kernelIdea: Multiplying two unit-circle points adds their angles, the defining law of an exponential, so cos θ + i sin θ is written e^{iθ}.

kernels.l1: Turn a quarter turn four times and you are facing the way you started.
kernels.l2: Multiplying by i turns you a quarter turn. Do it four times and you are back where you began: i, then −1, then −i, then 1, over and over.
kernels.l3: The powers of i repeat every four steps: i, −1, −i, 1. That repeating pattern is what makes the famous formula linking i to turning work — the four-step cycle sorts the terms into two separate families.
kernels.l4: Multiplying two points of the unit circle adds their angles. That is the same trade — adding on one side, multiplying on the other — that powers make, which is why turning by an angle gets written as a power. The four-step cycle of i is the simplest case of it.
kernels.l5: Multiplying two points of the unit circle adds their angles, which is exactly the trade a power makes: add the exponents, multiply the values. That is why cos θ + i sin θ is written as a power of e, and separating the two coordinates of that power is where the formula comes from.
kernels.l6: Multiplying two points of the unit circle adds their angles — the same trade of adding for multiplying that exponents make, which is why the circle points are written as a power.
kernels.l7: Multiplying two points of the unit circle adds their angles, which is exactly the law an exponential obeys. That shared law is what entitles cos θ + i sin θ to be written as a power of e.
kernels.l8: Euler’s formula is the identification of the complex exponential with the solution of y′ = iy, y(0) = 1; the series proof and the ODE proof are the same statement about the exponential map ℂ → ℂˣ.

kernel: Substituting iθ into the series for eˣ and using the cycle i, −1, −i, 1 separates into the cosine and sine series, giving e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ.
objectives: State the powers of i cycle
